title: From Supernovae to Dark Energy: How Do You Measure the Age of the Universe? - Heidelberg Laureate Forum - SciLogs - Wissenschaftsblogs
excerpt: Stuffing 14 billion years into 40 minutes is quite a challenge.
content:
No one really knows exactly when our ancestors began speaking. We can only estimate when our own species emerged. So how can anyone work out the age of the entire universe?

At the 2026 Heidelberg Laureate Forum, Nobel Prize-winning astronomer Brian P. Schmidt began with a more manageable answer. First, measure how fast the universe is expanding, then imagine running that expansion backwards. Galaxies that are now far apart were once closer together, so if you follow that motion far enough into the past, and you arrive at a time when the universe was extraordinarily dense, and can even reach the Big Bang.

Schmidt was delivering the Lindau Lecture, an annual guest lecture that reflects the close relationship between the Heidelberg Laureate Forum and the Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings. He warned the audience that compressing the history of the universe into around 40 minutes would be a rather lossy exercise, but then continued to explain how astronomers (including himself) uncovered some of the universe’s most striking secrets.

From Hubble to Schmidt

The starting point was Edwin Hubble’s observation that more distant galaxies appear to be moving away faster. The farther a galaxy is from Earth, the faster it moves away.

To establish the relationship, astronomers need two measurements: how far away a galaxy is and how much its light has been redshifted. As the universe expands, it stretches the light travelling through space, making its wavelengths longer and redder. More redshift means more stretching. Compare that with the galaxy’s distance, and astronomers can work out how quickly the universe is expanding today. We now call this the Hubble constant.

Schmidt measured that rate for his PhD. The figure he obtained was about 70 kilometres per second per megaparsec. That means for each additional megaparsec of distance, a galaxy’s recession speed increases by roughly 70 kilometres per second (a parsec is 3.26 light-years). With this rate of expansion, you can go back in time and get an estimate for the age of the universe.

“That straight extrapolation … tells you that the age of the universe is, give or take, 14 billion years,” Schmidt explained in the lecture.

Already, that is a pretty decent approximation. But it can only be an approximation.

For starters, it assumes that the expansion has proceeded at the same rate all along. That is unlikely to be the case, as gravity should have slowed it over time, and the contents of the universe affect its history.

To get a better estimate and understand what actually happened, astronomers needed to look into the past. Fortunately, looking far into space is looking into the past.

Light from a galaxy billions of light-years away has spent billions of years travelling towards us. If astronomers could measure distances and redshifts far enough away, they could compare the expansion rate then with the rate now.

For Schmidt, that became a challenge.

Hunting Explosions Across the Universe

Schmidt and colleagues got a bit of help from technology. “I was born at the right time,” the Nobel laureate joked.

In the 1990s, new digital cameras made it possible to search enormous numbers of distant galaxies for Type Ia supernovae. These are exceptionally bright stellar explosions, so bright that their light can be used to estimate how far away they are.

But finding the actual supernovae was not easy. Schmidt recalled spending nights working with 1,500 images. From those images, his team had to identify just a few promising explosions. Telescope time was scarce and the data strained the computers available to them. In addition, every newly discovered supernova had to be followed up quickly to measure its redshift. “We got six nights a year on these telescopes because it’s very competitive telescope time. So every photon counts,” Schmidt explained.

Existing software at the time narrowed the search somewhat, but it still left plenty of candidates. Schmidt joked that the team relied on a more old-fashioned version of neural networks: around 20 humans looking through the results. The painstaking search was necessary because supernovae are rare, and most of the apparent changes between images were something else.

Finding a promising explosion also started a race. The team had about 24 hours to pass its candidate from Chile to colleagues using the Keck telescope, which could measure its redshift. They needed both pieces of information – the supernova’s brightness to estimate its distance, and its redshift to measure how much the universe had expanded since its light set out.

Ultimately, though, they had a reliable dataset. The goal then was to measure how much gravity had slowed the universe’s expansion. Schmidt expected the distant supernovae to fall somewhere among the models in which matter pulls back on the expanding cosmos.

But they did not.

When the team plotted the distant explosions, they appeared farther away than expected in a universe whose expansion was slowing. The implication was startling but undeniable: expansion had been slower in the past than it is now. Instead of merely resisting gravity’s pull, the expansion of the universe was accelerating.

Basically, the universe is expanding at an accelerated rate.

Why? Well… That Is Another Question

The discovery earned Schmidt, Adam Riess, and Saul Perlmutter the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. It also helped astronomers finesse the age of the universe and estimate it with remarkable precision when accounting for this acceleration. Our current best estimates put the age of the universe at around 13.8 billion years old.

But, as it so often happens in science, answering one question brought many others.

Schmidt’s team had established that the universe’s expansion was accelerating. Explaining why is still one of cosmology’s biggest problems.

The leading model includes a cosmological constant: energy associated with empty space itself. In Einstein’s equations, it has a strange property called negative pressure, which can make expansion accelerate across vast distances. The model describes the universe remarkably well. This is the so-called “dark energy.” But despite an objectively spectacular name, dark energy remains a name for the effect astronomers measure, not an explanation of what produces it.

Other researchers are now following in Schmidt’s footsteps, attempting to bring more information about it. A leading question, for instance, is whether dark energy has behaved the same way throughout cosmic history.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, or DESI, maps millions of galaxies to track how expansion changed over billions of years. Its results, combined with other measurements, have produced intriguing hints that dark energy’s influence may have changed over time. This is still a very active field of research.

There is another unresolved mismatch. Measurements of nearby stars and supernovae give a higher value for today’s expansion rate than predictions based on light from the early universe. This has become known as the Hubble tension, and it raises the possibility that some important part of the cosmic story is missing.

Ultimately, Schmidt’s HLF lecture showed how vast conclusions can emerge from measurements of faint points of light. His team used distant supernovae to discover that the universe’s expansion was accelerating. Today, astronomers are using millions of galaxies to ask whether the dark energy invoked to explain that result has changed over time.

It is remarkable that we can estimate the universe’s age to remarkable precision. But as Schmidt’s lecture reminded us, the history of the universe is still being written, and so is our understanding of it.
